To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

asymptomatic bacteriuric strains of Escherichia (E.) coli suppress host gene expression through inhibition of RNA polymerase (RNAP) II, and that such bacterial modulation of host transcription may be a mechanism to promote bacterial colonization without causing disease.
asymptomatic bacteriuric strains of E. coli inhibit host gene expression and thereby prevent destructive inflammation in the urinary tract.

asymptomatic bacteriuric E. coli (ABU) strains suppress host RNA polymerase II (Pol II)–dependent gene expression in the urinary tract, and this inhibition of Pol II-dependent transcription may be a mechanism by which the bacteria promote tissue homeostasis and prevent destructive inflammation in the host.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how bacterial pathogens adapt to the host and cause disease.
the mechanisms by which bacteria modulate host gene expression to promote tissue integrity and inhibit pathology.
the mechanisms of bacterial adaptation and the role of commensal strains in the maintenance of host homeostasis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
bacterial modulation of host Pol II–dependent gene expression is essential to sustain asymptotic bacteriuria by ensuring that potentially damaging host responses will not occur.

asymptomatic bacteriuric strains of E. coli have evolved to modulate host gene expression through Pol II, which allows the bacteria to colonize the host without eliciting a destructive inflammatory response.

bacterial control of host gene regulation may constitute a general mechanism of bacterial commensal adaptation and that the lack of destructive immune activation in asymptomatic bacteriuric patients may reflect active suppression by ABU strains.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
asymptomatic bacteriuric (ABU) strains of E. coli have evolved mechanisms to suppress host responses, including RNA polymerase II (Pol II)–dependent gene expression.
asymptomatic bacteriuric strains of uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) suppress host inflammatory responses and tissue destruction by inhibiting the expression of RNA polymerase (Pol II)–dependent genes.
the asymptomatic bacteriuric E. coli strain 83972 inhibits RNA polymerase II-dependent host gene expression in the urinary tract, thereby suppressing pathogen-specific inflammation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
bacteria can manipulate host immune responses through suppression of host gene expression.
bacteria have the capacity to control the expression of host genes, and this is a mechanism that they have evolved to ensure their survival and to promote their colonization of the host.
bacterial control of host gene regulation may be an important mechanism by which commensal strains prevent the host from mounting a destructive immune response.
